title: 3  Background Information
text:
3.1 Three-phase Branch Power Matrix
NOTE: This file contains supporting matrix algebra and the fuller multiphase branch-flow formulation of Gan and Low (Gan and Low 2014). The working equations are in ch2_voltage_reactive_equations.qmd.
Recall that \(\mathbf{\bar V}_i\) and \(\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij}\) are \(3\times1\) column vectors. We previously used the per-phase complex power vector:
\[\mathbf{\bar s}_{ij}=\begin{bmatrix}P_{ij}^a+jQ_{ij}^a\\P_{ij}^b+jQ_{ij}^b\\P_{ij}^c+jQ_{ij}^c\end{bmatrix}\]
Gan and Low also use the full branch power matrix:
\[\mathbf{\bar S}_{ij}=\mathbf{\bar V}_i\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij}^{H} \tag{3.1}\]
Expanding the matrix multiplication:
\[
\mathbf{\bar S}_{ij}=
\begin{bmatrix}
\bar V_i^a(\bar I_{ij}^a)^* & \bar V_i^a(\bar I_{ij}^b)^* & \bar V_i^a(\bar I_{ij}^c)^*\\
\bar V_i^b(\bar I_{ij}^a)^* & \bar V_i^b(\bar I_{ij}^b)^* & \bar V_i^b(\bar I_{ij}^c)^*\\
\bar V_i^c(\bar I_{ij}^a)^* & \bar V_i^c(\bar I_{ij}^b)^* & \bar V_i^c(\bar I_{ij}^c)^*
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Note that the diagonal elements are the conventional complex powers for each phase:
\[\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{\bar S}_{ij})=\mathbf{\bar s}_{ij}\]
The off-diagonal elements are cross-phase voltage-current products. They do not represent extra downstream branches or separate real/reactive phase powers. The full \(3\times3\) matrix is useful for Gan and Low’s branch-flow and optimization formulations, but it is not required just to substitute phase power into KVL.

title: 3  Background Information
section: 3.2 Derive the Magnitude of the Voltage
text:
3.2 Derive the Magnitude of the Voltage
Following the same approach as in Equation 4.21, we can obtain squared voltage magnitudes using the three-phase KVL equation:
\[\mathbf{\bar V}_j=\mathbf{\bar V}_i-\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij}\]
To retain all cross-phase voltage products, multiply the equation on the right by its Hermitian transpose:
\[\mathbf{\bar V}_j\mathbf{\bar V}_j^H=(\mathbf{\bar V}_i-\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij})(\mathbf{\bar V}_i-\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij})^H \tag{3.2}\]
The Hermitian transpose, denoted by \(H\), means conjugate transpose; it does not mean extracting the diagonal. A \(3\times1\) voltage vector times its \(1\times3\) conjugate transpose produces a \(3\times3\) matrix.

3.2.1 Solving for the left hand side of Equation 3.2
\[
\mathbf{\bar V}_j\mathbf{\bar V}_j^{H}
=\begin{bmatrix}\bar V_j^a\\\bar V_j^b\\\bar V_j^c\end{bmatrix}_{3\times1}
\begin{bmatrix}(\bar V_j^a)^*&(\bar V_j^b)^*&(\bar V_j^c)^*\end{bmatrix}_{1\times3}
=\begin{bmatrix}
|\bar V_j^a|^2&\bar V_j^a(\bar V_j^b)^*&\bar V_j^a(\bar V_j^c)^*\\
\bar V_j^b(\bar V_j^a)^*&|\bar V_j^b|^2&\bar V_j^b(\bar V_j^c)^*\\
\bar V_j^c(\bar V_j^a)^*&\bar V_j^c(\bar V_j^b)^*&|\bar V_j^c|^2
\end{bmatrix}_{3\times3}
\tag{3.3}\]
Note that the diagonal elements are squared voltage magnitudes. The off-diagonal elements remain complex cross-phase voltage products.
Gan and Low define the voltage matrix as:
\[\mathbf{\bar W}_j=\mathbf{\bar V}_j\mathbf{\bar V}_j^H \tag{3.4}\]
Similarly:
\[\mathbf{\bar W}_i=\mathbf{\bar V}_i\mathbf{\bar V}_i^H \tag{3.5}\]


3.2.2 Solving for the right hand side of Equation 3.2
We can apply the same Hermitian transpose to the right-hand side:
\[\mathbf{\bar W}_j=(\mathbf{\bar V}_i-\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij})(\mathbf{\bar V}_i^H-\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij}^H\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}^H)\]






NoteVoltage Eq. Note



\[(\mathbf{\bar Z}\mathbf{\bar I})^H=\mathbf{\bar I}^H\mathbf{\bar Z}^H\]
The multiplication order reverses because \((AB)^H=B^HA^H\). This is a property of the conjugate transpose, not merely a rule for fixing dimensions.


Expanding the right-hand side:
\[\mathbf{\bar W}_j=\mathbf{\bar V}_i\mathbf{\bar V}_i^H-\mathbf{\bar V}_i\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij}^H\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}^H-\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar V}_i^H+\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij}^H\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}^H \tag{3.6}\]
We previously defined the voltage matrix in Equation 3.5 and the branch-power matrix in Equation 3.1. Accordingly, we can define the current outer-product matrix as:
\[\mathbf{\bar L}_{ij}=\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij}^H\]
Therefore, Equation 3.6 can be written as:
\[\boxed{\mathbf{\bar W}_j=\mathbf{\bar W}_i-\mathbf{\bar S}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}^H-\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar S}_{ij}^H+\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar L}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}^H} \tag{3.7}\]






NoteNote



Equation 3.7 is an exact squared-voltage matrix relationship derived from KVL. The term \(\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar L}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}^H\) is quadratic in line current; it is the outer product of the line voltage-drop vector with itself. Its diagonal is not the same as the real-power loss. For our immediate voltage–reactive-power work, the per-phase power equations and KVL are sufficient as starting equations, so we can keep this fuller derivation for background.






Gan, Lingwen, and Steven H Low. 2014. “Convex Relaxations and Linear Approximation for Optimal Power Flow in Multiphase Radial Networks.” 2014 Power Systems Computation Conference, 1–9.

title: 4  Equations Derivation
text:
4.1 Deriving the Real and Reactive Power Equations
NOTE: Baran and Wu use the DistFlow equations for a balanced, single-phase equivalent radial distribution system. We use these equations as a starting point for our unbalanced three-phase work.
Consider the following single line diagram:
For each load, we consider \(P_{L,n}\) and \(Q_{L,n}\), indicating real and reactive power consumed at bus \(n\). Positive load means consumption.
Each line has an impedance, \(\bar{Z}_{n} = r_{n}+jx_{n}\). The sending-end complex power flow on each line is given by:
\[\bar{S}_{n} = P_{n}+jQ_{n}\]
For instance, for the line leaving bus \(i+1\):
\[\bar{S}_{i+1} = P_{i+1}+jQ_{i+1}\]
I think it is easier to see this if we look at the power flow between two consecutive buses. Consider the power flow between buses \(n\) and \(n+1\). We define \(P_n\) as the power leaving bus \(n\) and entering line \((n,n+1)\):
\[\underbrace{P_{n}}_{\text{Power leaving bus $n$}} = \underbrace{P_{n,loss}}_{\text{Line loss}} + \underbrace{P_{n+1}}_{\text{Power leaving bus $n+1$}} + \underbrace{P_{L,n+1}}_{\text{Load at bus $n+1$}} \tag{4.1}\]

title: 4  Equations Derivation
text:
4.1.1 Decomposing the Losses term in equation Equation 4.1
\[P_{loss} = r |I|^{2}\]
At any given bus \(n\):
\[P_{n,loss} = r_{n} |I_{n}|^{2} \tag{4.2}\]
Recall:
\[\bar{S} = \bar{V}\bar{I}^{*} = P+jQ\]
Wherein the magnitude of the apparent power is given by:
\[|S| = |I|~|V| = \sqrt{P^{2} + Q^{2}}\]
Squaring both sides:
\[|S|^{2} = |I|^{2}~|V|^{2} = P^{2}+Q^{2}\]
Solving for the squared current magnitude:
\[|I|^{2} = \frac{P^{2} + Q^{2}}{|V|^{2}}\]
For the line leaving bus \(n\), the squared current magnitude is:
\[|I_{n}|^{2} = \frac{P^{2}_{n} + Q^{2}_{n}}{|V_{n}|^{2}} \tag{4.3}\]
substituting the current equation Equation 4.3 into Equation 4.2 we get:
\[P_{n,loss} = r_{n} \frac{P^{2}_{n} + Q^{2}_{n}}{|\bar{V}_{n}|^{2}} \tag{4.4}\]
Substituting Equation 4.4 in the power balance between buses \(n\) and \(n+1\) in Equation 4.1, we get:
\[\underbrace{P_{n}}_{\text{Power leaving bus $n$}} = \underbrace{r_{n} \frac{P^{2}_{n} + Q^{2}_{n}}{|\bar{V}_{n}|^{2}}}_{\text{Line loss}} + \underbrace{P_{n+1}}_{\text{Power leaving bus $n+1$}} +\underbrace{P_{L,n+1}}_{\text{Load at bus $n+1$}} \tag{4.5}\]






NoteNote



Equation 4.5 is the real power DistFlow Equation. This is the exact branch real-power balance for the single-phase equivalent line model, assuming the bus has one downstream line and no additional injection. For a branching feeder, we also account for every outgoing branch.


Similarly, the reactive power can be calculated in a similar manner:
\[\underbrace{Q_{n}}_{\text{Q leaving bus $n$}} = \underbrace{x_{n} \frac{P^{2}_{n} + Q^{2}_{n}}{|\bar{V}_{n}|^{2}}}_{\text{Reactive power absorbed in the line}} + \underbrace{Q_{n+1}}_{\text{Q leaving bus $n+1$}} +\underbrace{Q_{L,n+1}}_{\text{Q consumed by bus $n+1$ load}} \tag{4.6}\]

title: 4  Equations Derivation
text:
4.2 Deriving the Voltage Equation:
Applying KVL to buses, \(i\) and \(i-1\) in Figure 4.1:
\[\bar{V}_{i-1} = \bar{Z}_{i-1}~\bar{I}_{i-1} + \bar{V}_{i} \tag{4.7}\]
The current complex value can be solved for in a similar manner as in equation Equation 4.3:
\[\bar{V}_{n}~\bar{I}_{n}^{*} = P_{n}+jQ_{n}\]
Taking the complex conjugate and solving for \(\bar{I}_{n}\):
\[\bar{I}_{n} = \frac{P_{n}-jQ_{n}}{\bar{V}_{n}^{*}} \tag{4.8}\]
Substituting Equation 4.8 in Equation 4.7 & solving for \(\bar{V}_{i}\):
\[\bar{V}_{i} = \bar{V}_{i-1} - \bar{Z}_{i-1}~\bar{I}_{i-1} \tag{4.9}\]
\[\bar{V}_{i} = \bar{V}_{i-1} - \bar{Z}_{i-1}~\frac{P_{i-1}-jQ_{i-1}}{\bar{V}_{i-1}^{*}}\]
We can then extend this to get only the magnitude of the voltage:
Recall \(|a-b|^{2} = (a-b)(a^{*}-b^{*})\):
\[|\bar{V}_{i}|^{2} = (\bar{V}_{i-1} - \bar{Z}_{i-1}~\bar{I}_{i-1})~(\bar{V}^{*}_{i-1} - \bar{Z}^{*}_{i-1}~\bar{I}^{*}_{i-1})\]
Multiplying both terms, we end up with:
\[|\bar{V}_{i}|^{2} = |\bar{V}_{i-1}|^{2} - 2~\Re \{\underbrace{\bar{V}^{*}_{i-1}~\bar{I}_{i-1}}_{\substack{\text{Apparent} \\ \text {Power} \\ \text{Conjugate}}}~\bar{Z}_{i-1}\} + |\bar{Z}_{i-1}|^{2}~|\bar{I}_{i-1}|^{2} \tag{4.10}\]
Recall \(\bar{S}^{*}_{i-1} = \bar{V}^{*}_{i-1}~\bar{I}_{i-1} = P_{i-1} - jQ_{i-1}\)
So the middle term can be decomposed such that:
\[\bar{V}^{*}_{i-1}~\bar{I}_{i-1}~\bar{Z}_{i-1} = (P_{i-1} - jQ_{i-1})(r_{i-1}+jx_{i-1})\]
Multiplying and obtaining only the real part because we are trying to calculate the magnitude:
\[\Re \{\bar{Z}_{i-1}~\bar{V}^{*}_{i-1}~\bar{I}_{i-1}\} = r_{i-1}~P_{i-1} + x_{i-1}~Q_{i-1} \tag{4.11}\]
The last term in Equation 4.10 can be simplified further. Recall that \(|\bar{Z}_{i-1}|^{2} = r^{2}_{i-1} + x^{2}_{i-1}\) and \(|\bar{I}_{i-1}|^{2} = \frac{P^{2}_{i-1}+Q^{2}_{i-1}}{|\bar{V}_{i-1}|^{2}}\)
\[|\bar{Z}_{i-1}|^{2}~|\bar{I}_{i-1}|^{2} = (r^{2}_{i-1} + x^{2}_{i-1})~(\frac{P^{2}_{i-1}+Q^{2}_{i-1}}{|\bar{V}_{i-1}|^{2}}) \tag{4.12}\]
Substituting Equation 4.11 and Equation 4.12 in Equation 4.10:
\[|\bar{V}_{i}|^{2} = |\bar{V}_{i-1}|^{2} - 2(r_{i-1}~P_{i-1} + x_{i-1}~Q_{i-1})+(r^{2}_{i-1} + x^{2}_{i-1})~\frac{P^{2}_{i-1}+Q^{2}_{i-1}}{|\bar{V}_{i-1}|^{2}} \tag{4.13}\]
Note that Equation 4.13 is essentially: \[|\bar{V}_{i}|^{2} = |\bar{V}_{i-1}|^{2} - 2(r_{i-1}~P_{i-1} + x_{i-1}~Q_{i-1})+\underbrace{(r^{2}_{i-1} + x^{2}_{i-1})}_{\text{Imedance }Z^{2}}\underbrace{~\frac{P^{2}_{i-1}+Q^{2}_{i-1}}{|\bar{V}_{i-1}|^{2}}}_{\text{Current }I^{2}}\]
\(V = ZI\), making the last term a loss term. This loss term is a second order contribution associated with line losses. Assuming the losses insignificant, we can drop this term and the equation becomes:
\[|\bar{V}_{i}|^{2} = |\bar{V}_{i-1}|^{2} - 2(r_{i-1}~P_{i-1} + x_{i-1}~Q_{i-1})\]
Rearranging the equation:
\[(|\bar{V}_{i}|^{2} - |\bar{V}_{i-1}|^{2}) \approx 2(r_{i-1}~P_{i-1} + x_{i-1}~Q_{i-1})\]
Recall \(a^{2} - b^{2} = (a-b)(a+b)\):
\[(|\bar{V}_{i}| - |\bar{V}_{i-1}|)(|\bar{V}_{i}| + |\bar{V}_{i-1}|) \approx 2(r_{i-1}~P_{i-1} + x_{i-1}~Q_{i-1})\]
Defining the voltage drop as: \(\Delta V = |\bar{V}_{i-1}| - |\bar{V}_{i}|\):
\[\Delta V(|\bar{V}_{i}| + |\bar{V}_{i-1}|) \approx 2(r_{i-1}~P_{i-1} + x_{i-1}~Q_{i-1})\]
Solving for \(\Delta V\):
\[\Delta V \approx \frac{2(r_{i-1}~P_{i-1} + x_{i-1}~Q_{i-1})}{(|\bar{V}_{i}| + |\bar{V}_{i-1}|)}\]
Assuming the voltage difference between adjascent buses is small:
\[|\bar{V}_{i}| \approx |\bar{V}_{i-1}| \approx V\]
Therefore,
\[|\bar{V}_{i}| + |\bar{V}_{i-1}| \approx 2V\]
substituting in the previous \(\Delta V\) equation:
\[\Delta V \approx \frac{2(r_{i-1}~P_{i-1} + x_{i-1}~Q_{i-1})}{2V}\]
Cancelling the 2:
\[\Delta V \approx \frac{r_{i-1}~P_{i-1} + x_{i-1}~Q_{i-1}}{V} \tag{4.14}\]






NoteNote



Equation 4.13 is the Voltage Magnitude DistFlow Equation. This equation applies exactly to each branch under the paper’s single-phase equivalent series-impedance model. It does not, by itself, describe mutual coupling in an unbalanced three-phase system.

title: 4  Equations Derivation
5  Motivation
text:
5.1 State of the Art
Distribution voltage is conventionally held near nominal along the primary feeder, typically within ±5%, so that every customer receives a service voltage inside ANSI C84.1 Range A (114–126 V). The limit, however, applies at the customer service point, not on the primary. If residential inverters can correct the voltage locally at each household, the primary feeder voltage no longer has to be chosen to protect the worst-placed customer. It becomes a decision variable: it can be lowered for conservation voltage reduction (CVR) or raised to reduce losses, while inverters hold each household within its service limit.

title: 5  Motivation
text:
CVR with smart inverters. Smart inverters have been coordinated with tap changers, regulators and capacitors to achieve CVR on three-phase unbalanced feeders (jha2019bilevel?; zhang2019distributed?), including integrated primary-secondary networks with voltage-dependent loads (zhang2021primarysecondary?). In these studies inverters support CVR, while the primary voltage stays within its conventional band.
Grid-edge voltage control. Dedicated utility-owned devices on the secondary side of service transformers regulate customer voltage so that the primary can be lowered further. Field deployments report up to 5% CVR (moghe2016gridedge?), limiting-node voltage increases of 0.88–2.04% (jha2023gridedge?), and energy savings up to 4.7% when combined with smart inverters (padullaparti2023cvr?).
Volt-VAR curve design. Per-inverter Volt-VAR rules have been optimized for single-phase feeders (murzakhanov2024optimal?), unbalanced multiphase feeders (gupta2025regulating?), and a single utility-scale battery (ingebrigtsen2026optimizing?). All aim to keep voltages near nominal rather than to compensate a deliberately shifted primary.
Cross-phase coupling. On unbalanced four-wire networks, reactive power injected on one phase changes the voltages on the other phases (wang2020interphase?; dalal2024crossphase?).
Siting and sizing. Methods exist to choose how many voltage-support units are needed and where, but for balanced networks (giannitrapani2017optimal?) or PV at medium voltage (chen2022optimal?).

title: 5  Motivation
text:
5.2 Research Gap
Existing work either regulates customer voltage at the grid edge with dedicated utility devices, or uses residential inverters as auxiliary support while the primary voltage remains within its conventional band. No study has treated the primary feeder voltage as a free decision variable whose feasible range is set by the corrective capability of customer-owned residential inverters.
In particular, it is not known:

how far the primary voltage can be shifted, up or down, before participating inverters can no longer hold every household within its service-voltage limit;
how this range depends on the number, location and phase of participating inverters, and how it is reduced by cross-phase coupling, non-participating customers and battery operating state on unbalanced feeders;
whether the energy saved by operating the primary away from nominal outweighs the additional losses caused by the reactive power needed to compensate it; and
whether the required compensation can be delivered autonomously through location-dependent Volt-VAR settings.

We define the decoupling range as the set of primary-side voltage set-points for which the participating inverters can keep every household service voltage within its target limits.

title: 5  Motivation
text:
5.3 Research Goal
To develop and evaluate a methodology for inverter-enabled grid-edge voltage regulation, in which residential inverters compensate their local service voltage so that the primary feeder voltage can be decoupled from customer voltage limits on unbalanced distribution networks.

title: 5  Motivation
text:
5.4 Research Objectives

O1 — Quantify the decoupling range. Develop a sensitivity-based model that determines the decoupling range as a function of inverter count, location, phase assignment and rating.
O2 — Identify the limiting factors. Characterize how cross-phase coupling, non-participating customers and battery operating state (charging, discharging, idle) narrow or extend the decoupling range.
O3 — Evaluate the net benefit. Determine the primary voltage set-point that maximizes net benefit across loading conditions, accounting for voltage-dependent load reduction, additional network losses, transformer loading and substation power factor.
O4 — Enable decentralized implementation. Translate the required reactive power into location-dependent Volt-VAR settings (reference voltage, deadband, slope and reactive limits). Identify when autonomous operation is sufficient and when coordination is needed.

title: 5  Motivation
text:
5.5 Research Questions
RQ1 — Decoupling feasibility: For a given set of residential inverters, what range of primary voltage set-points can be supported while keeping every household within its target service voltage, and how does this range scale with inverter count, location, phase assignment and rating?
RQ2 — Limiting factors: How do cross-phase coupling, non-participating customers and battery operating state constrain the decoupling range on unbalanced feeders?
RQ3 — Net benefit: Within the feasible range, which primary voltage set-point maximizes net energy benefit, after netting voltage-dependent load reduction against additional losses, and how does this optimum change with loading?
RQ4 — Decentralized implementation: Can the reactive power required at each location be encoded in Volt-VAR curves that hold household voltages at their targets without communication, and under what conditions does coordination become necessary?

title: 5  Motivation
text:
5.6 Scope and Assumptions

Unbalanced three-phase feeders with service transformers and single-phase residential connections. To decide: test feeder (e.g., IEEE 8500-node or a PNNL taxonomy feeder) and whether secondaries are modelled as split-phase.
Customer-owned single-phase residential inverters (PV and battery) with reactive capability limited by IEEE 1547-2018.
Voltage-dependent load models (ZIP or CVR factor), since CVR savings depend directly on them.
Quasi-static time-series simulation over representative loading conditions.

title: 5  Motivation
text:
5.7 Expected Contributions

The concept and quantification of a decoupling range for inverter-enabled grid-edge voltage regulation, and its dependence on inverter participation, location and phase.
An analysis of how cross-phase coupling and battery operating state limit grid-edge compensation on unbalanced feeders.
A net-benefit assessment identifying when shifting the primary voltage is worthwhile once added losses are included.
A method for deriving location-dependent Volt-VAR settings that implement the approach autonomously. Volt-VAR curves are the implementation of the methodology, not its primary objective.

Verification

Transformer Voltage:

\(r = 0.01~p.u.\)

\(S = 50~kVA\)
\(Q \in \{-5,0,5\}~kVAr\)

Therefore:
Calculating the base \(\mathbf{z}\) value: \[Z_{base} = \frac{V_{base}^{2}}{S_{base}} = \frac{(240)^{2}~V}{50~KVA} = 1.15~\Omega\]
Then the actual \(\mathbf{x}\) becomes:
\[x_{actual} = 0.06~p.u. \times 1.15~\Omega=0.069~\Omega\]
Calculating the actual \(\mathbf{r}\) value:
\[r_{actual} = 0.01~p.u. \times 1.15~\Omega=0.0115~\Omega\]
Since only reactive power is being injected, we can neglect \(P\) and \(r\) Plugging in values in the \(\Delta V\) equation:
\[\Delta V = \frac{RP+XQ}{V} \approx \frac{XQ}{V}\] \[\Delta V = \frac{(0.069~\Omega)(5~kVAr)}{240~V} = 1.44~V\]
Converting the voltage back to per unit:
\[V_{p.u.} = \frac{V_{act}}{V_{base}} = \frac{1.44~V}{240~V} \approx 0.006 \approx 0.6\%\]
Note that the \(50~kVA\) is at the transformer, not house 15.


Understanding the Jacobian used in this experiment

The Jacobian describes how small changes in the assumed bus voltages change the calculated electrical quantities. To interpret the matrix printed by GridLAB-D, we first need to identify those voltage values and the quantities the solver is trying to balance.

Step 1: Describe one voltage using two numbers
Chapter 2 uses a complex voltage, written as \(\bar V\). The house-15 leg-1 voltage in the zero-\(Q\) case at 20:46 is
\[
\bar V_{15}=108.363349-j6.272459\ \mathrm{V}.
\]
This voltage has a real part, \(108.363349\) V, and an imaginary part, \(-6.272459\) V. The subscripts \(R\) and \(I\) identify these two parts:
\[
V_R=108.363349\ \mathrm{V},\qquad V_I=-6.272459\ \mathrm{V},
\]
so the same voltage can be written as
\[
\bar V=V_R+jV_I.
\]
This is the rectangular representation of the voltage. The magnitude and angle provide another representation of exactly the same voltage:
\[
|\bar V_{15}|=108.544733\ \mathrm{V},\qquad
\delta_{15}=-3.312789^{\circ}.
\]
GridLAB-D’s solver in this experiment works with the real and imaginary parts. A conventional angle/magnitude power-flow calculation works with the magnitude and angle instead. The physical voltage is the same; the two calculations use different pairs of numbers to describe it.
The notation \(e+jf\) means \(V_R+jV_I\): \(e\), which is the real part and \(f\) is the imaginary part. We will use \(V_R\) and \(V_I\) here to make their meanings visible.
The notation \(\operatorname{Im}\{\bar V\}\) means take the imaginary part of the voltage. Thus:
\[
\operatorname{Im}\{\bar V_{15}\}=-6.272459\ \mathrm{V}.
\]


Step 2: Calculate the specified current and the current mismatch
The specified power at a connection is generation minus load consumption:
\[
\bar S_{\mathrm{specified}}
=(P_{\mathrm{inverter}}-P_{\mathrm{house}})
+j(Q_{\mathrm{inverter}}-Q_{\mathrm{house}}).
\]
Using the current iteration’s voltage estimate, chapter 2’s complex-power equation gives the specified device current:
\[
\bar I_{\mathrm{specified}}
=\frac{\bar S_{\mathrm{specified}}^{*}}{\bar V^{*}}
=\frac{(P_{\mathrm{inverter}}-P_{\mathrm{house}})
-j(Q_{\mathrm{inverter}}-Q_{\mathrm{house}})}{\bar V^{*}}.
\]
This is the net current injected by the devices at the connection. Generation is positive; consumption is negative. For constant-power devices, the power is specified, but the current is recalculated using the voltage estimate at each iteration.
For example, a single 120 V connection with a 1,200 W load, no reactive demand, and no inverter generation has
\[
\bar I_{\mathrm{specified}}=\frac{-1200}{120}=-10\ \mathrm{A}.
\]
The negative value means that the house consumes current rather than injecting it. This example uses one 120 V connection; the actual house model has two legs, so \(240~V\).
The network also determines a current from the assumed bus voltages. At house 15, the current leaving through the service line is
\[
\bar I_{\mathrm{network},15}
=\frac{\bar V_{15}-\bar V_{\mathrm{tap15}}}{\bar Z_{\mathrm{service15}}}.
\]
For a connection with several lines, the network current is the sum of the currents leaving through those lines.
The current mismatch (instead of power mismatch) is specified device injection minus calculated network current:
\[
\boxed{\Delta\bar I=\bar I_{\mathrm{specified}}-\bar I_{\mathrm{network}}.}
\]
Continuing the 1,200 W example, if the assumed voltages give \(\bar I_{\mathrm{network}}=-9\) A, then
\[
\Delta\bar I=(-10)-(-9)=-1\ \mathrm{A}.
\]
If the network current is \(-10\) A, the mismatch is zero and current balance is satisfied. Collecting the real and imaginary mismatches at all connections produces the current mismatch vector.
The ordinary power-flow mismatch vector compares specified and calculated powers:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
\Delta P_i\\ \Delta Q_i
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
P_{i,\mathrm{specified}}-P_{i,\mathrm{calculated}}\\
Q_{i,\mathrm{specified}}-Q_{i,\mathrm{calculated}}
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The current-injection formulation instead compares specified and network currents. Written with the imaginary components first, matching our GridLAB-D block arrangement, this is
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
\Delta I_{i,Im}\\ \Delta I_{i,R}
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
I_{i,Im,\mathrm{specified}}-I_{i,Im,\mathrm{network}}\\
I_{i,R,\mathrm{specified}}-I_{i,R,\mathrm{network}}
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Both parts should be approximately zero when the currents balance. The calculation below shows this for house 15.
Worked calculation: house 15 at 20:46, with inverter Q = 0
We start with the solved zero-Q case, before changing the inverter output. Every voltage and current below refers to one balanced 120 V leg equivalent. We do not mix whole-house power with a single-leg voltage.
1. Read the house power. In the zero-Q simulation file, house 15 has
constant_power_12 6623.66668249131+0j;
This is the whole-house load across the 240 V connection:
\[
P_{\mathrm{house}}=6623.666682\ \mathrm{W},\qquad
Q_{\mathrm{house}}=0\ \mathrm{var}.
\]
For the balanced single-leg calculation, divide the house power equally between the two legs:
\[
P_{\mathrm{house,leg}}=\frac{6623.666682}{2}
=3311.833341\ \mathrm{W},\qquad
Q_{\mathrm{house,leg}}=0\ \mathrm{var}.
\]
Initially the inverter has \(P_{\mathrm{inv}}=0\) W and \(Q_{\mathrm{inv}}=0\) var, so its contribution to either leg is zero.
2. Read the house voltage and take its conjugate. The zero-Q voltage at house 15 is
\[
\bar V_{15}=108.363349-j6.272459\ \mathrm{V}.
\]
The specified-current equation uses the conjugate of this voltage. Taking the conjugate changes the sign of the imaginary part:
\[
\bar V_{15}^{*}=108.363349+j6.272459\ \mathrm{V}.
\]
3. Calculate the specified current. Substituting the single-leg power and voltage gives
\[
\bar I_{\mathrm{specified},15}
=\frac{(0-3311.833341)-j(0-0)}{108.363349+j6.272459}
=\frac{-3311.833341}{108.363349+j6.272459}.
\]
Dividing the complex numbers gives
\[
\boxed{\bar I_{\mathrm{specified},15}
\approx-30.460244+j1.763148\ \mathrm{A}.}
\]
The denominator is voltage, not line impedance. This current comes from the specified device power and the house-voltage estimate.
4. Read the neighboring tap voltage and service-line impedance. House 15 connects to tap 15 through the 30 ft service line:
tap 15 ---- service_15 ---- house 15
The voltage at tap 15 is
\[
\boxed{\bar V_{\mathrm{tap15}}=108.463828-j6.246562\ \mathrm{V}.}
\]
This is a different connection from house 15. Their voltages are close because the service line is short: their magnitudes are approximately 108.644 V and 108.545 V, respectively.
For the same balanced single-leg equivalent, the service impedance is
\[
\boxed{\bar Z_{15}=0.0032386364+j0.0010376674\ \Omega.}
\]
This is the impedance of service_15 only, not the whole path from the transformer. It is the balanced-leg equivalent obtained from the model’s exported impedance matrix, as used in the chapter-2 verification script.
5. Calculate the network current. Current leaving house 15 toward tap 15 is
\[
\bar I_{\mathrm{network},15}
=\frac{\bar V_{15}-\bar V_{\mathrm{tap15}}}{\bar Z_{15}}.
\]
These voltages are used directly, without taking their conjugates. First subtract their real parts:
\[
108.363349-108.463828=-0.100479\ \mathrm{V}.
\]
Then subtract their imaginary parts:
\[
-6.272459-(-6.246562)=-0.025897\ \mathrm{V}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\bar V_{15}-\bar V_{\mathrm{tap15}}
=-0.100479-j0.025897\ \mathrm{V}.
\]
Dividing this voltage difference by the service impedance gives
\[
\bar I_{\mathrm{network},15}
=\frac{-0.100479-j0.025897}
{0.0032386364+j0.0010376674}
\approx-30.460147+j1.763243\ \mathrm{A}.
\]
This closely matches the specified current. Both currents use the same convention: current injected into the network, or leaving the house through the service line, is positive.
6. Calculate the current mismatch. Subtract network current from specified current:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta\bar I_{15}
&=\bar I_{\mathrm{specified},15}-\bar I_{\mathrm{network},15}\\
&\approx(-30.460244+j1.763148)-(-30.460147+j1.763243)\\
&\approx-0.000097-j0.000095\ \mathrm{A}
\approx0.
\end{aligned}
\]
The small remaining difference reflects the precision of the printed voltages and impedances. These inputs came from a solved operating point, so the specified current and network current should agree approximately. Rounded to two decimal places, both are \(-30.46+j1.76\) A.
The house powers, branch voltages and impedances for this calculation are recorded in gld/verify_ch2/branch_measurements.csv, selecting q_injected_kvar = 0 and branch = service_15 for the service-line values. The house demand is specified in gld/results/house15_q_sweep/q_+00000var/case.glm.


Step 3: Use the current mismatch to correct the voltages
The Jacobian relates voltage corrections to the current mismatch. The Newton–Raphson calculation is
\[
\boxed{\mathbf J^{(k)}\Delta\mathbf V^{(k)}=\Delta\mathbf I^{(k)}.}
\]
Here, \(k\) identifies the current iteration. The vector \(\Delta\mathbf I^{(k)}\) contains the current mismatches just calculated. The vector \(\Delta\mathbf V^{(k)}\) contains the real and imaginary voltage corrections. After solving for those corrections, the voltages are updated:
\[
\mathbf V^{(k+1)}=\mathbf V^{(k)}+\Delta\mathbf V^{(k)}.
\]
GridLAB-D then recalculates the currents and mismatches using the updated voltages. This repeats until the solver’s convergence checks are satisfied.
The Jacobian accounts for how both network current and specified device current change with voltage. Its entries are derivatives of network current minus specified device current, with respect to the voltage components. The entries have units A/V. This includes the voltage dependence of constant-power device current.
All connected voltage corrections are calculated together. For example, changing house-15 voltage changes service-line current at both house 15 and tap 15.


Step 4: Identify what TCIM means
TCIM is the three-phase current-injection method. It is the name of GridLAB-D’s current-balance power-flow formulation. It can also handle the single-phase and split-phase connections in this model; the name does not mean that every connection in this experiment has three phases.
The settings solver_method NR and NR_solver_algorithm TCIM describe two related choices:

TCIM identifies the equations and voltage representation: current balance using real/imaginary voltage components.
NR identifies how those equations are solved: repeated Newton–Raphson voltage corrections.

Consequently, the printed matrix describes changes in current mismatch caused by changes in real/imaginary voltage, rather than changes in \(P\) and \(Q\) caused by changes in voltage angle and magnitude.


Step 5: Write the full Jacobian with each quantity defined
First, consider the conventional power-flow Jacobian used when discussing \(\mathbf J_4\). The quantities involved are:







Symbol
Meaning




\(\mathbf P\)
List of calculated real-power injections at the included connections


\(\mathbf Q\)
List of calculated reactive-power injections at those connections


\(\boldsymbol\delta\)
List of voltage angles


\(\mathbf v\)
List of voltage magnitudes, \(v_i=|\bar V_i|\)



Power injection is positive for generation and negative for consumption. Bold symbols collect values from multiple connections into vectors. Each Jacobian entry is a partial derivative: one quantity changes while the other independent voltage variables remain fixed.
The four blocks are
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf J_{PQ}=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf J_1 & \mathbf J_2\\
\mathbf J_3 & \mathbf J_4
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial\mathbf P}{\partial\boldsymbol\delta}
&\dfrac{\partial\mathbf P}{\partial\mathbf v}\\[6pt]
\dfrac{\partial\mathbf Q}{\partial\boldsymbol\delta}
&\dfrac{\partial\mathbf Q}{\partial\mathbf v}
\end{bmatrix}.
}
\tag{6.1}\]
For a Newton calculation, \(\Delta\mathbf P\) and \(\Delta\mathbf Q\) are the specified power injections minus the injections calculated from the current voltage estimate. The required voltage corrections satisfy
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf J_1 & \mathbf J_2\\
\mathbf J_3 & \mathbf J_4
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
\Delta\boldsymbol\delta\\ \Delta\mathbf v
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\Delta\mathbf P\\ \Delta\mathbf Q
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
In particular, \((\mathbf J_4)_{15,15}\) describes how calculated \(Q_{15}\) changes with house-15 voltage magnitude while all angles and other magnitudes remain fixed. The inverter sweep does not hold those other quantities fixed. Its measured voltage response therefore cannot be obtained by simply taking the reciprocal of that one entry. The other blocks also participate in the voltage response.
For GridLAB-D, the voltage variables are the real and imaginary components, rather than magnitude and angle. The mismatch vector contains imaginary-current mismatches first and real-current mismatches second when grouped into the following block form:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{bmatrix}
\Delta\mathbf I_{Im}\\
\Delta\mathbf I_R
\end{bmatrix}
=
\underbrace{
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf A & \mathbf B\\
\mathbf C & \mathbf D
\end{bmatrix}
}_{\mathbf J_{\mathrm{TCIM}}}
\begin{bmatrix}
\Delta\mathbf V_R\\
\Delta\mathbf V_{Im}
\end{bmatrix}.
}
\tag{6.2}\]
The subscript \(R\) identifies real parts, and \(Im\) identifies imaginary parts. Each block describes a particular current/voltage relationship:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf A&=\frac{\partial(\mathbf I_{\mathrm{network},Im}-\mathbf I_{\mathrm{specified},Im})}{\partial\mathbf V_R},
&\mathbf B&=\frac{\partial(\mathbf I_{\mathrm{network},Im}-\mathbf I_{\mathrm{specified},Im})}{\partial\mathbf V_{Im}},\\[6pt]
\mathbf C&=\frac{\partial(\mathbf I_{\mathrm{network},R}-\mathbf I_{\mathrm{specified},R})}{\partial\mathbf V_R},
&\mathbf D&=\frac{\partial(\mathbf I_{\mathrm{network},R}-\mathbf I_{\mathrm{specified},R})}{\partial\mathbf V_{Im}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The specified-minus-network current mismatch is on the left of Equation 6.2. The Jacobian describes the voltage corrections needed to close that difference. The blocks describe current/voltage derivatives; \(\mathbf D\) is not the conventional \(\mathbf J_4=\partial\mathbf Q/\partial\mathbf v\).
For a three-bus system with one fixed slack bus and two single-phase PQ buses, the four voltage corrections belong to buses 2 and 3:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
\Delta I_{2,Im}\\
\Delta I_{3,Im}\\
\Delta I_{2,R}\\
\Delta I_{3,R}
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf A & \mathbf B\\
\mathbf C & \mathbf D
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
\Delta V_{2,R}\\
\Delta V_{3,R}\\
\Delta V_{2,Im}\\
\Delta V_{3,Im}
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Each block is \(2\times2\), so this non-slack system is \(4\times4\). The current mismatches are calculated from the current voltage estimate, and the voltage corrections are added to obtain the next estimate.
In this three-bus example, the Jacobian matrix becomes:

\[
\underbrace{
\left[
\begin{array}{cc|cc}
\frac{\partial I_{2,Im}}{\partial V_{2,R}} &
\frac{\partial I_{2,Im}}{\partial V_{3,R}} &
\frac{\partial I_{2,Im}}{\partial V_{2,Im}} &
\frac{\partial I_{2,Im}}{\partial V_{3,Im}} \\[10pt]
\frac{\partial I_{3,Im}}{\partial V_{2,R}} &
\frac{\partial I_{3,Im}}{\partial V_{3,R}} &
\frac{\partial I_{3,Im}}{\partial V_{2,Im}} &
\frac{\partial I_{3,Im}}{\partial V_{3,Im}} \\ \hline
\frac{\partial I_{2,R}}{\partial V_{2,R}} &
\frac{\partial I_{2,R}}{\partial V_{3,R}} &
\frac{\partial I_{2,R}}{\partial V_{2,Im}} &
\frac{\partial I_{2,R}}{\partial V_{3,Im}} \\[10pt]
\frac{\partial I_{3,R}}{\partial V_{2,R}} &
\frac{\partial I_{3,R}}{\partial V_{3,R}} &
\frac{\partial I_{3,R}}{\partial V_{2,Im}} &
\frac{\partial I_{3,R}}{\partial V_{3,Im}}
\end{array}
\right]
}_{\displaystyle J =
\left[\begin{smallmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{smallmatrix}\right]}
\]

The source voltage is fixed. GridLAB-D nevertheless retains its two positions in the exported matrix. It uses large diagonal entries (\(10^{10}\) in this dump) and skips source-voltage updates during the normal solve. Those rows are special source constraints, rather than ordinary unknown-bus current-balance equations. Excluding the source’s two fixed voltage components would leave 126 values to solve for.
The matrix is square because it supplies one equation for each stored voltage component. If all real voltage components were placed first and all imaginary components second, its four blocks would each be \(64\times64\).
The raw CSV instead stores components together by bus. At a split-phase bus, its columns are ordered as
\[
[V_{R,1},\ V_{R,2},\ V_{I,1},\ V_{I,2}],
\]
and its current-mismatch rows are ordered as
\[
[\Delta I_{1,Im},\ \Delta I_{2,Im},\ \Delta I_{1,R},\ \Delta I_{2,R}].
\]
Consequently, the four global derivative blocks cannot be extracted simply by cutting the raw CSV into four equal rectangles. The rows and columns first need to be grouped according to their meanings.
